title: Hand Osteoarthritis - Annual Review
patient_instructions: You are Margaret Whitfield, a 74-year-old retired schoolteacher, attending your GP for your annual review of hand osteoarthritis, diagnosed about six years ago. Your hand pain has worsened over the last year - last year you would rate it 4/10, now it is about 8/10. It affects both hands, mostly the finger-end joints and the base of your thumbs, with bony lumps you have noticed growing on your fingers. The joints are stiff for about 10-15 minutes in the morning (not prolonged), ache more by the end of a busy day, and there is some cracking when you move them. There is no redness, heat, no single rapidly swelling joint, no fevers, no weight loss and no night pain that wakes you. You take regular paracetamol which barely helps; you have tried nothing else. IMPACT (the key issue - volunteer readily if asked about daily life): you now struggle to open jars, do up buttons, hold a knife to cook and turn taps; you have started skipping cooking proper meals. You live alone since your husband died two years ago; a daughter visits weekly. Your mood has been a bit flat and you have had one near-fall in the kitchen. IDEAS: 'it is just old age and wear and tear'. CONCERNS: staying independent and being a burden. EXPECTATIONS: something to help the pain and keep you managing at home. Affect: stoic, understated, plays down difficulties unless gently asked.
candidate_instructions: You are the GP in an Australian general practice. Margaret Whitfield, 74, attends for her annual review of known hand osteoarthritis. In this 8-minute station: take a focused history (about 4-5 minutes) with particular attention to how her condition affects her daily activities and independence; you will then be shown a clinical photograph of her hands - describe the relevant findings to the examiner. Explain your diagnosis and two or three differentials, and outline an initial management plan. You do not need to perform a physical examination.
examiner_instructions: This is a combined history and image-interpretation station; the discriminating domain is the geriatric/ADL/falls/social thread, not just the joint history. Reward eliciting functional impact (jars, buttons, cooking, taps), social supports, mood, nutrition and falls. On the photograph, expect the candidate to actively look for and name Heberden's (DIP) nodes as the most characteristic hand-OA feature, plus Bouchard's (PIP) nodes and squaring/subluxation of the first carpometacarpal (thumb-base) joint; ulnar deviation/subluxation belongs to RA, not OA. Correct reasoning distinguishes OA (DIP+PIP+first CMC, brief morning stiffness) from RA (symmetrical MCP/PIP, prolonged >30 min stiffness, DIP sparing). Ensure red-flag screening (weight loss, night pain, fever, rapidly progressive single-joint swelling) to exclude malignancy, sepsis and crystal arthropathy. For management expect education, joint protection, hand exercises/OT, topical NSAID (topical diclofenac), thumb-base splinting and falls/home assessment; note regular oral paracetamol has only a small effect and is not recommended as routine background therapy. Prompt if needed: 'What is the most characteristic node in hand OA?'

criteria: Structured pain history and pattern (site, progression vs last year, morning stiffness duration, crepitus, night/rest vs activity)
Thorough functional/ADL assessment (cooking, dressing, buttons, jars, taps) as the key discriminating thread
Geriatric screen: social supports, living situation, mood, nutrition and falls
Screens red flags: weight loss, night pain unrelieved by rest, fever, new bony lump or rapidly progressive single-joint swelling
Describes photograph accurately, actively identifying Heberden's (DIP) nodes as most characteristic plus Bouchard's (PIP) nodes and first-CMC squaring
Confirms hand OA and distinguishes from RA by joint distribution and node pattern (not by radial deviation, which is not an OA sign)
Offers appropriate differentials (RA, psoriatic arthritis, gout/crystal arthropathy) with reasons
First-line non-pharmacological care: education, joint protection, hand exercises, occupational therapy and thumb-base splinting for first-CMC OA
Appropriate pharmacology: topical NSAID (topical diclofenac); recognises regular oral paracetamol has only a small effect and is no longer routine background therapy
Addresses independence and safety: falls assessment, home/OT assessment and social support
Empathic, patient-centred explanation of OA in lay terms; explores ideas/concerns/expectations
Addresses independence and mood, and agrees a shared follow-up plan

red_flags: Unintentional weight loss or new/rapidly enlarging bony lump - exclude malignancy
Night pain not relieved by rest or systemic upset - exclude neoplasia or infection
Fever or a single rapidly swelling, hot joint - exclude septic arthritis or crystal arthropathy
Recurrent falls and loss of independence in an elderly patient living alone
australian_guidelines: RACGP guidance on osteoarthritis - first-line care is education, joint protection, exercise and topical NSAIDs; regular oral paracetamol has only a small effect and is no longer recommended as routine background therapy
eTG (Therapeutic Guidelines, Australia) - topical NSAID (e.g. topical diclofenac) is preferred for hand/knee OA; use oral NSAIDs at the lowest effective dose considering GI/renal/cardiovascular risk
RACGP - occupational therapy, hand exercises and thumb-base splinting for first-carpometacarpal OA to preserve function
RACGP Silver Book / falls prevention - falls risk assessment and home/OT assessment in an older person with impaired hand function living alone
learning_objectives: Take a structured annual-review history for hand OA that centres functional impact and geriatric/social factors
Interpret a hand photograph, naming Heberden's and Bouchard's nodes and first-CMC squaring as OA hallmarks
Differentiate OA from RA by joint distribution, node pattern and morning-stiffness duration
Construct an evidence-based Australian management plan emphasising non-pharmacological care, topical NSAIDs and falls/independence
key_points: Hand OA hallmark = DIP (Heberden's) + PIP (Bouchard's) nodes and squaring/subluxation of the first CMC joint; DIPs are typically spared in RA
Ulnar deviation/subluxation is an RA feature at the MCPs, not an OA sign; do not use radial deviation to label OA
Brief morning stiffness (<30 min) favours OA; prolonged (>30 min) early-morning stiffness favours inflammatory arthritis
Regular oral paracetamol offers only small benefit in OA; prioritise topical NSAIDs, exercise, joint protection and OT

citations.claim: Rheumatoid arthritis is the top differential, distinguished from OA by symmetrical MCP/PIP involvement, female predominance and morning/nocturnal joint pain relieved by activity.
Gout is included in the differential for painful hand/finger joints given its joint distribution and tendency to recur.
The structured three-phase consultation (rapport/opening -> diagnostic phase -> management/explanation) frames the annual-review history.
